body: A teammate missed yesterday's project meeting. What is the most helpful thing to do?
options: Complain about it to the team lead
Send them a short summary of the decisions and their tasks
Leave it; catching up is their job
Quietly do their tasks without telling them
explanation: A quick summary keeps everyone aligned and avoids duplicate or missed work.

body: A group member has not replied for two days and the deadline is close. What should you do first?
options: Message them politely, check they are okay and confirm their part; tell the team if there is still no reply
Remove their name from the project
Complain about them in the class group
Wait silently until the deadline
explanation: Start with a respectful check-in. Escalate only if it does not work, and keep the team informed.

body: The team chose another member's idea instead of yours. What is the best response?
options: Refuse to help with it
Keep bringing your idea up in every meeting
Secretly build your own version
Support the chosen idea and help make it work
explanation: Once a team decides, committing to the decision matters more than whose idea it was.

body: A new teammate is struggling with their Excel task. What should you do?
options: Joke about it with others
Do it yourself and tell the teacher they did nothing
Offer to show them the basics or share a short guide
Tell them to leave the team
explanation: Helping a teammate build the skill helps the whole team, now and later.

body: What should a team do at the start of a project?
options: Start working alone without discussing
Agree together on the goal, roles and deadlines
Each pick only the easiest task
Wait for someone to tell them everything
explanation: A shared plan avoids confusion, overlap and last-minute surprises.

body: You realise you will miss your deadline by one day. What should you do?
options: Tell the team early, explain why, and propose a new plan
Say nothing and hope no one notices
Blame another member
Submit unfinished work without telling anyone
explanation: Early warning gives the team time to adjust. Hiding delays makes them worse.

body: Two teammates start arguing loudly during a meeting. What is the best thing to do?
options: Immediately take one person's side
Leave the meeting
Record the argument and share it
Suggest a short pause and help each person explain their point calmly
explanation: Calming things down and hearing both sides moves the team back to the work.

body: Your team project went well. What is the best way to respond?
options: Take most of the credit yourself
Say nothing
Thank everyone and mention each person's contribution
Point out who did the least
explanation: Recognising everyone's work builds trust for the next project.

body: What is the best way to keep everyone updated on who is doing what?
options: Remembering it all yourself
A shared task list that everyone can see
Telling only the team leader
Updating everyone once at the end
explanation: A visible tracker shows progress and gaps without extra meetings.

body: A teammate says your slides look cluttered. What is the best response?
options: Thank them, ask what would help, and improve the slides
Defend every slide
Stop making slides for the team
Ignore the feedback
explanation: Feedback is information. Asking questions turns it into specific improvements.

body: A teammate does good work but keeps missing meetings because of a part-time job. What is the best approach?
options: Report them to the faculty right away
Keep them out of decisions
Cancel all meetings and let everyone work alone
Agree on a meeting time or written updates that work for everyone
explanation: Adjusting how the team communicates keeps a contributing member included.

body: One member is doing most of the work and seems stressed. What should you do?
options: Let them continue, since the work is getting done
Give them the remaining tasks too, since they are fastest
Check in with them privately and help share out the tasks
Tell the faculty the team is failing
explanation: Uneven workload burns people out and leaves the team exposed if that person drops out.

body: You disagree with your team lead's plan. What is the best approach?
options: Quietly follow your own plan instead
Explain your concern with reasons and a suggestion, then go with the final decision
Discuss your doubts with other members but not the lead
Agree in the meeting and then do the minimum
explanation: Raising concerns openly gives the lead a chance to improve the plan, and committing afterwards keeps the team united.

body: You notice a teammate's section is copied from a website. What should you do?
options: Raise it privately, explain the risk, and help rewrite it in your own words with sources
Submit it anyway, since it is their section
Point it out in the class group chat
Delete their section without telling them
explanation: Handling it privately protects the team's work and the teammate's dignity.

body: The team chat is full of off-topic messages and important updates get lost. What should you do?
options: Leave the group
Ask the leader to remove the people posting jokes
Repeat every update several times
Suggest a pinned message or a separate group just for project updates
explanation: A clear channel for decisions keeps information easy to find without spoiling the friendly chat.

body: A quiet teammate rarely speaks in meetings. What is the best approach?
options: Assume they have nothing to add
Give them only small tasks
Ask for their view directly and kindly, or invite written input
Tell them in front of everyone to speak up
explanation: Some people contribute better when invited or when they can write. Their ideas still count.

body: You finish your part of the project early. What should you do?
options: Relax and stop checking messages
Ask the team if anyone needs help, or offer to review others' work
Start an unrelated side project
Redo other people's parts without asking
explanation: Spare time spent helping or reviewing improves the final result for everyone.

body: A teammate's mistake cost the team marks. What is the best response?
options: Discuss as a team what went wrong and how to avoid it, without blaming
Explain to the faculty that it was their fault
Avoid working with them again
Pretend it did not happen
explanation: Focusing on the fix rather than the person helps the team improve and stay together.

body: Your team has members from different departments with very different ideas. What works best?
options: Let the largest department decide
Split into separate mini-projects
Go with whoever argues best
Use each person's strengths and combine the ideas
explanation: Mixed teams do well when different skills are combined rather than ranked.

body: In a placement group discussion, another candidate interrupts you. What should you do?
options: Talk over them to finish your point
Stay silent for the rest of the discussion
Let them finish, then calmly continue your point
Point out their rudeness to the panel
explanation: Panels notice composure and respect. Calmly coming back to your point shows both.

body: The deadline is tomorrow and two tasks are still unassigned. What should you do?
options: Wait for someone to volunteer
Propose who takes which task based on availability and confirm it in the chat
Do both yourself without telling anyone
Ask for an extension without trying
explanation: Clear ownership, confirmed in writing, is what gets unclaimed work done.

body: A teammate shares an idea you think will not work. What is the best response?
options: Ask questions about it and explain your concern respectfully
Say directly that it is a bad idea
Agree, to avoid conflict
Change the topic
explanation: Questions often show whether an idea can work, and keep the discussion respectful.

body: Two members argue about whether to use Google Docs or Microsoft Word for the report. What is the best way to settle it?
options: Let the more senior member choose
Use both and merge at the end
Ask the faculty to decide
Compare both quickly against what the team needs, such as live editing and access, and decide together
explanation: Deciding by shared criteria ends the argument and leads to a better choice than seniority or splitting.

body: A teammate tells you privately that a family problem is making them fall behind. What should you do?
options: Tell the team the reason so they understand
Report them to the faculty for not contributing
Respect their privacy, offer flexible help, and adjust tasks without sharing the reason
Keep their workload the same to be fair to others
explanation: Supporting them while keeping their confidence helps both the person and the project.

body: Your team lead keeps changing the requirements at the last minute. What is the best approach?
options: Stop working until they decide
Suggest agreeing on the requirements by a set date and writing them down
Complain to the other members
Keep working to the old requirements
explanation: An agreed, written scope protects the team's time and still lets the lead decide.

body: During an internship, a senior asks you to do something that seems to go against company policy. What should you do?
options: Politely ask for clarification and check the policy or with your manager before acting
Do it, because a senior asked
Refuse firmly and report the senior to HR straight away
Do it but keep a record in case of trouble
explanation: Asking first is respectful and protects you and the company. It may also be a misunderstanding.

body: Your team has two strong members who both want to lead. What is the best arrangement?
options: Let them compete; the better one will win
Vote for one leader and ask the other to step back
Rotate the leader every day
Agree on separate areas each one owns and on how final decisions are made
explanation: Clear ownership and a decision rule use both people's strengths without constant conflict.

body: For the final presentation, a member who contributed little wants to present the most. What should you do?
options: Let them present everything to avoid an argument
Refuse to present with them
Plan the speaking parts so each person presents what they worked on
Tell the evaluator they did little
explanation: Matching speakers to the work makes the talk stronger and is fair to everyone.

body: In a team review, you must give feedback on a friend's weak work. What is the best approach?
options: Praise it so you do not hurt them
Give specific, kind, honest feedback with suggestions
Point out the problems in front of the whole team
Stay quiet and let someone else say it
explanation: Specific, kind feedback helps your friend improve and protects the team's work.

body: Your team works remotely from different cities and updates often get missed. What works best?
options: Agree on a short fixed check-in time and a shared written update
Message whenever something comes up
Send all updates only to the leader
Meet for two hours every day
explanation: A predictable rhythm and a written record keep a remote team in sync without wasting time.
